lessonTitle: Neurological Examination: Cranial Nerves, Power, Tone, Reflexes and Motor Neuron Patterns

blocks.text: A 63-year-old man wakes with a weak right arm and leg and a drooping right side of the mouth, but he can still wrinkle his forehead. Before any scan, a bedside examination of his face, tone, power and reflexes can tell you whether the lesion is in the brain or in the peripheral nerve.

blocks.markdown: The neurological examination turns symptoms into a **site of lesion**. It follows a fixed order so that nothing is omitted: cranial nerves, then the limbs (inspection, tone, power, reflexes, coordination, sensation), then gait. This unit covers the cranial nerve examination, grading of power on the **MRC scale**, testing of tone and reflexes, and the interpretation of findings as an **upper motor neuron (UMN)** or **lower motor neuron (LMN)** pattern. Sensory testing and coordination are introduced but are not the focus here.

blocks.title: Upper and lower motor neurons
blocks.text: Upper motor neurons run from the motor cortex through the internal capsule and brainstem to the spinal cord (the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts). Lower motor neurons have their cell bodies in the anterior horn of the spinal cord (or brainstem motor nuclei) and run in peripheral nerves to muscle. Damage at different levels produces different, characteristic signs.

blocks.markdown:
### Examining the cranial nerves

Explain and obtain consent, sit the patient comfortably, and test each nerve in order, comparing the two sides.

- **I (olfactory)**: smell, only if indicated.
- **II (optic)**: visual acuity, visual fields by confrontation, pupillary light reflexes and fundoscopy.
- **III, IV, VI (oculomotor, trochlear, abducens)**: eye movements by following a finger in an H pattern, asking about double vision, and noting nystagmus and ptosis.
- **V (trigeminal)**: light touch over the three divisions of the face (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular), the corneal reflex if indicated, and the muscles of mastication (clench the jaw).
- **VII (facial)**: raise the eyebrows, close the eyes tightly, show the teeth, puff out the cheeks.
- **VIII (vestibulocochlear)**: hearing (whisper test; tuning fork tests of Rinne and Weber if indicated).
- **IX, X (glossopharyngeal, vagus)**: say 'ahh' and watch the palate rise symmetrically, and listen to the voice and cough.
- **XI (accessory)**: shrug the shoulders and turn the head against resistance.
- **XII (hypoglossal)**: put out the tongue and watch for deviation, wasting and fasciculations.

rows: Upper motor neuron (e.g. stroke affecting the corticobulbar fibres)
The upper face receives bilateral cortical input, so the other hemisphere compensates
Lower motor neuron (e.g. Bell's palsy, facial nerve lesion)
Weak, cannot wrinkle or close the eye
All facial muscles on that side lose their only supply
blocks.caption: Distinguishing upper and lower motor neuron facial weakness.

blocks.title: Reading the face and tongue
blocks.prompt: A 70-year-old woman has a drooping left mouth. She can raise both eyebrows equally and close both eyes. Her tongue deviates slightly to the left on protrusion with no wasting. What does this suggest?

steps.text: Face: weakness of the lower face with preserved forehead movement means the upper face is spared, which is the pattern of an upper motor neuron facial weakness.
Reason: the forehead muscles have bilateral cortical innervation, so a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion spares them. A lower motor neuron lesion would weaken the forehead too.

Tongue: with a supranuclear (UMN) lesion the tongue deviates away from the side of the cortical lesion, towards the weak side. Her left facial droop suggests a right-sided hemisphere lesion, and the tongue deviating left (towards the weak side) fits that pattern.
No wasting or fasciculations of the tongue, which would suggest a lower motor neuron lesion of the hypoglossal nerve.

blocks.answer: A right-sided supranuclear (upper motor neuron) lesion, such as a stroke, rather than a peripheral facial nerve lesion.

blocks.markdown:
### Examining the limbs: tone, power and reflexes

Inspect first for wasting, fasciculations (twitching of muscle fibres at rest), abnormal movements and posture.

**Tone**: the resistance felt when you move a relaxed limb passively. Take the wrist or elbow, and the knee or ankle, and move them at different speeds. Increased tone may be **spasticity** (velocity-dependent, with a clasp-knife quality; UMN lesion) or **rigidity** (uniform throughout the movement, 'lead-pipe', with or without cogwheeling, as in parkinsonism). Decreased tone (**hypotonia**) occurs with LMN lesions.

**Power**: test each major movement against resistance, comparing sides, and grade on the **MRC scale**.

rows: Movement against gravity but not against resistance
Movement against gravity and some resistance (may be subdivided 4-, 4, 4+)
blocks.caption: The Medical Research Council (MRC) scale for muscle power.

blocks.markdown: **Reflexes**: use a tendon hammer with the limb relaxed and positioned symmetrically. Compare sides. Reinforcement (Jendrassik manoeuvre) can bring out a reduced reflex. Commonly tested reflexes with their main root values are the biceps (C5-6), supinator (C5-6), triceps (C7), knee (L3-4) and ankle (S1-2). Grades range from absent, through normal, to brisk, with sustained **clonus** (rhythmic contractions on sudden stretch) marking an upper motor neuron lesion. Test the **plantar response** by stroking the lateral sole: a normal response is flexion of the great toe, and an **upgoing great toe (extensor plantar, Babinski sign)** in an adult indicates an upper motor neuron lesion.

rows: Weakness in the distribution of the nerve or root
Normal, or wasting late from disuse
blocks.caption: Comparing upper and lower motor neuron signs.

blocks.title: Classifying a pattern of findings
blocks.prompt: A 58-year-old man has weakness of the left foot. On examination the left leg has marked wasting of the calf, visible fasciculations, reduced tone, absent ankle reflex, MRC grade 3 dorsiflexion and a flexor plantar response. Is this an upper or lower motor neuron pattern?

steps.text: List the features: wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone, absent reflex, flexor plantar.
Match to the table: wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia and a flexor or absent plantar are all lower motor neuron features.
No upper motor neuron features are present: there is no spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus or extensor plantar.
Grade the power: dorsiflexion is MRC 3, meaning movement against gravity but not against any resistance.

blocks.answer: A lower motor neuron pattern (damage to the anterior horn cell, nerve root or peripheral nerve), with dorsiflexion power MRC grade 3.

blocks.title: Patterns point to the lesion site
blocks.text: UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, extensor plantar, no wasting) point to a lesion in the brain or spinal cord. LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia, reduced reflexes) point to a lesion of the anterior horn cell, root or peripheral nerve. Mixed signs can occur, for example in motor neurone disease.

blocks.title: Reporting your findings
blocks.text: State findings in a standard form: 'Tone in the right arm is increased with a clasp-knife quality; power is MRC 4 in shoulder abduction and 3 in wrist extension; reflexes are brisk; the plantar response is extensor.' Then conclude with the pattern and site.

points: Examine cranial nerves I to XII in order, comparing sides; facial weakness that spares the forehead is upper motor neuron.
Tone: spasticity (clasp-knife) in UMN lesions, rigidity in parkinsonism, hypotonia in LMN lesions.
Power is graded 0 to 5 on the MRC scale; 3 means movement against gravity but not resistance.
Reflexes are brisk with clonus and an extensor plantar in UMN lesions; reduced with wasting and fasciculations in LMN lesions.
Combine the findings into an upper or lower motor neuron pattern to localise the lesion.

questions.stem: A patient is asked to push their arm against resistance and can move the limb through full range against gravity and against moderate resistance, but the examiner can overcome the effort. What is the MRC grade?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: movement against gravity and some resistance is grade 4.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: grade 2 is movement with gravity eliminated.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: grade 3 is movement against gravity only, without resistance.

questions.explanation: Grade 4 on the MRC scale means movement against gravity and some resistance, but not full strength. Grade 3 would fail against any resistance, and grade 5 is normal.

questions.stem: Which description corresponds to MRC grade 2 power?

options.text: Movement is possible only with gravity eliminated
A flicker of contraction without movement
Movement against gravity but not against resistance
No contraction

questions.correctOptionText: Movement is possible only with gravity eliminated
questions.explanation: The MRC scale rises from no contraction (0) through a flicker (1) to movement with gravity eliminated (2), against gravity (3), against resistance (4) and normal (5).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a left facial droop affecting the lower face with the forehead spared. Which pattern of lesion does this indicate?

options.text: Upper motor neuron lesion of the facial pathway
Lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve
Lesion of the trigeminal nerve
Lesion of the hypoglossal nerve

questions.correctOptionText: Upper motor neuron lesion of the facial pathway

distractorRationale.a: Correct: forehead sparing reflects bilateral cortical input to the upper face.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: LMN lesion weakens the whole half of the face including the forehead.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the trigeminal nerve supplies sensation and mastication, not facial expression.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue.

questions.explanation: The upper face receives corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, so a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion spares the forehead. A facial nerve (LMN) lesion affects the forehead as well.

questions.stem: Which combination of findings in the right leg indicates an upper motor neuron lesion?

options.text: Increased tone, brisk knee reflex, sustained ankle clonus and an extensor plantar response
Decreased tone, absent reflexes, wasting and fasciculations
Normal tone with a loss of sensation in a stocking distribution
Reduced tone with a flexor plantar response and wasting

questions.correctOptionText: Increased tone, brisk knee reflex, sustained ankle clonus and an extensor plantar response

distractorRationale.c: Wrong: describes a sensory neuropathy, not a motor neuron pattern.

questions.explanation: UMN lesions release spinal reflexes, causing spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus and an extensor plantar response. LMN lesions cause the opposite pattern with wasting and fasciculations.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has an absent knee jerk with the other reflexes present. What simple manoeuvre can be used to confirm that the reflex is truly absent and not just weak?

options.text: Reinforcement, such as asking the patient to clench their hands (Jendrassik manoeuvre)
Asking the patient to close their eyes
Testing the plantar response
Increasing the force of the hammer to the maximum

questions.correctOptionText: Reinforcement, such as asking the patient to clench their hands (Jendrassik manoeuvre)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: reinforcement can bring out a reduced reflex.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this does not reinforce a reflex.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: excessive force is uncomfortable and does not improve reliability.

questions.explanation: Reinforcement increases motor neuron excitability and can elicit a reflex that is only reduced. A reflex that remains absent after reinforcement is classed as absent.

questions.stem: Sustained ankle clonus is a sign of a lower motor neuron lesion.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Sustained clonus is a sign of an upper motor neuron lesion because of the loss of descending inhibition. Lower motor neuron lesions reduce or abolish reflexes.

questions.stem: On asking a patient to open their mouth and say 'ahh', the examiner sees the uvula deviate to the right while the left side of the palate fails to rise. Which pair of cranial nerves is being tested?

options.text: Glossopharyngeal and vagus
Trigeminal and facial
Accessory and hypoglossal
Oculomotor and abducens

distractorRationale.a: Correct: palatal elevation tests IX and X.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: V and VII test facial sensation and expression.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: XI tests shoulder shrug and XII the tongue.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: III and VI test eye movements.

questions.explanation: Saying 'ahh' tests the palate and uvula, supplied by the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. The uvula deviates away from the side of the weak palate.

questions.stem: Describe how you would examine and report the tone and power of the right arm of a patient, including the MRC scale.
markingGuide: Inspect for wasting and fasciculations and compare sides
Tone: passive movement at different speeds, noting spasticity, rigidity or hypotonia
Power: test each movement against resistance, comparing sides
MRC scale 0 to 5 with the meaning of the key grades
Report in a standard form with the muscle group and grade
Explain the task and obtain consent
questions.explanation: Tone and power are tested systematically and reported with a recognised scale so that changes can be tracked. MRC grades give a comparable record of strength.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has weakness of the right arm and leg. Describe the examination findings that would indicate an upper motor neuron pattern and contrast them with a lower motor neuron pattern.
markingGuide: UMN: increased tone (spasticity), brisk reflexes, clonus, extensor plantar, little wasting
LMN: reduced tone, reduced or absent reflexes, wasting, fasciculations, flexor or absent plantar
UMN weakness in a pyramidal distribution
Site of lesion: brain or spinal cord for UMN; anterior horn cell, root or peripheral nerve for LMN
Mentions facial forehead sparing as a UMN sign when the face is involved
questions.explanation: UMN and LMN lesions cause opposite effects on tone and reflexes because the descending pathways modulate spinal reflex arcs. Recognising the pattern localises the lesion.

questions.stem: Outline the structured examination of the cranial nerves, stating one test for each of nerves II, V, VII, XI and XII.
markingGuide: Explains and obtains consent, compares both sides
II: visual acuity, fields, pupillary reflexes or fundi
V: facial sensation in three divisions or jaw clench
VII: raise eyebrows, close eyes, show teeth, puff cheeks
XI: shrug shoulders or turn head against resistance
XII: tongue protrusion looking for deviation, wasting or fasciculations
questions.explanation: A structured cranial nerve examination tests each nerve with a specific manoeuvre, comparing the two sides. Following numerical order ensures none is omitted.
